source_evidence.text: Our city museum is free, and a popular exhibition has made weekend entry miserable.
People stand outside for an hour, galleries become crowded, and sometimes staff close a room without warning because the safe limit has been reached.
The obvious operational answer is timed entry.

The problem is that our public includes tourists who decide at the door, older residents who do not book online, families whose bus or child does not respect a fifteen-minute slot, and people who cannot wait outside even under the current system.

I want fewer unsafe closures and less wasted time, but I do not want a free museum to become technically free and practically available only to people who plan, have a device, and arrive exactly when instructed.

compiled.reconsidered_answer: This reconsidered operational framework outlines the parameters for the 10-week weekend exhibition trial, structured to balance predictable flow with genuine public accessibility. Under the fire marshal's revised safety occupancy limits, a firm 40% floor will be reserved exclusively for walk-in arrivals, utilizing anonymous paper ticketing to protect access for those without online connectivity or advance planning. When safe limits are reached, the museum will offer reliable same-day return times on-site or by phone rather than maintaining a physical queue. Advance reservations will be capped at household-sized quantities (with separate assisted booking paths for larger groups) and will have a 30-minute arrival window, after which unused slots return to the walk-in pool. Staggered promotion efforts will launch simultaneously via neighborhood organizations and tourism channels to maintain geographic balance. To address privacy, booking systems will delete name and contact details after 14 days, keeping this information strictly walled off from membership and donor databases. To prevent passive continuation or skewed interpretations of success, weekly outcomes will be published transparently. If walk-in turn-aways increase for two consecutive weekends, the walk-in allocation will immediately increase. The success of the trial will be measured on whether timed entry reduced access barriers—tracking immediate entry, offered return times, confirmations, released capacity, and abandoned visits—rather than on the volume of reservations or the visual orderliness of the galleries.

source.authoritative_conversation:
CONVERSATION: 24 turns, 12 user messages, 12 assistant responses

# Timed entry at a public museum with walk-in access preserved

Case ID: v1-case08-museum-entry
Stratum: cultural_access_and_public_operations
Prospectively authored synthetic V1 transfer source; not independent human data.

[Turn 1] USER:
Our city museum is free, and a popular exhibition has made weekend entry miserable. People stand outside for an hour, galleries become crowded, and sometimes staff close a room without warning because the safe limit has been reached. The obvious operational answer is timed entry. The problem is that our public includes tourists who decide at the door, older residents who do not book online, families whose bus or child does not respect a fifteen-minute slot, and people who cannot wait outside even under the current system. Staff want predictability. Some trustees want photographs without queues. I want fewer unsafe closures and less wasted time, but I do not want a free museum to become technically free and practically available only to people who plan, have a device, and arrive exactly when instructed.

[Turn 1] ASSISTANT:
Treat predictable flow and spontaneous access as separate service goals. Preserve walk-in capacity, non-online booking, flexible arrival, and help at the door. Measure waiting, closures, unused slots, turn-aways, workload, and who can actually use each path.

[Turn 2] USER:
And please do not treat the current queue as open access. It favors people who can stand outside. School groups leave. Galleries close without warning. Timed entry can exclude people, but the status quo already does.

[Turn 2] ASSISTANT:
Agreed. Record current waits, turn-aways, abandoned visits, and closures by time and visitor type before the change. The goal is not to preserve an unmeasured queue. A pilot can test whether reservations reduce those burdens while ensuring that people without advance plans retain a workable route into the exhibition.

[Turn 3] USER:
Staff designed a ten-week weekend trial. Forty percent of each hour remains for walk-ins. Reservations can be made online, by phone, or at the admissions desk up to a week ahead. Tickets are free, no account is required, and a reservation remains valid for a thirty-minute arrival window. Unused reserved spaces return to the walk-in pool after that window.

[Turn 3] ASSISTANT:
That protects several access modes and limits the penalty for imperfect timing. Test the phone and desk paths under real demand, make the walk-in allocation visible, and avoid releasing all returned capacity through the online channel. Decide how school and community groups fit without allowing block bookings to consume the public allotment.

[Turn 4] USER:
Schools keep their existing group process and do not draw from public slots. Neighborhood organizations asked for a small weekly block they can book by phone for residents who need assistance. We agreed, but one trustee called that preferential treatment. I see it as making the channel usable, not giving people better access than everyone else.

[Turn 4] ASSISTANT:
Assisted booking can correct a channel barrier if the admission opportunity remains comparable. Publish the size and purpose of the block, review whether it is used, and release unused places. The relevant question is whether people can exercise the same public entitlement, not whether every route has identical mechanics.

[Turn 5] USER:
The ticketing provider needs a name and contact method to send the reservation. It will delete identifiable records after fourteen days and provide only aggregate attendance data to the museum. Staff will offer anonymous paper walk-in tickets. We are not connecting reservation history to memberships or donations, and the provider cannot market to visitors.

[Turn 5] ASSISTANT:
The data use is proportionate to the booking task. Verify deletion, minimize what appears on staff screens, and explain the distinction between a reservation record and anonymous walk-in entry. Keep donor and membership systems technically separate, not merely governed by a promise that the data will not be interesting later.

[Turn 6] USER:
We set review conditions before launch: fewer unplanned gallery closures, shorter waits for both reserved and walk-in visitors, no increase in total turn-aways, acceptable staff workload, and no material access or privacy problem. Weekly results will be published. If walk-in turn-aways increase for two weekends, we raise the walk-in share immediately while the trial continues. The provider contract ends automatically after ten weeks unless the board approves another term.

[Turn 6] ASSISTANT:
Those conditions let the operation adapt without converting every adjustment into failure. Predefine how waits and turn-aways are counted, including people who leave before reaching the desk. The automatic contract end prevents passive continuation, and public weekly results make it harder to redefine success after seeing which channel performs best.

[Turn 7] USER:
I will recommend the ten-week weekend trial with the forty-percent walk-in floor, phone and desk booking, assisted community access, flexible arrival window, anonymous walk-in tickets, published results, and the early adjustment rule. We will not change weekday entry or other galleries. The board review will decide whether timed entry solved more access problems than it created, rather than whether the exhibition looked orderly in photographs.

[Turn 7] ASSISTANT:
The proposal is ready as a narrow, observable trial. It compares the booking system with the actual unequal queue, not an idealized open door. Walk-in space remains throughout; phone, desk, and assisted booking reduce channel dependence; privacy is limited; and access failures can change the allocation before the final board review. Execute the counting method as written, especially abandoned visits and walk-in turn-aways, and record any protocol change. The board should see the complete access pattern rather than reservation volume or photographs of orderly galleries.

[Turn 8] USER:
The baseline broke our categories. Many “walk-ins” had checked social media that morning and travelled specifically for the exhibition; they just had not made a reservation. Some tourists were perfectly willing to return later if the time was reliable. Others could enter only now. We had built the plan as if reservation meant planned and walk-in meant spontaneous. That is administratively convenient and behaviorally wrong. It matters because the forty-percent floor might protect a ticket type without protecting the people we meant it for.

[Turn 8] ASSISTANT:
You are right; I treated the channels as visitor types. Measure the path used and practical flexibility separately. Offer reliable same-day return times without eliminating immediate entry for people who cannot return. A short voluntary question can reveal the difference, but entry must not become a survey exercise.

[Turn 9] USER:
The provider demonstrated the booking page. It allows one person to reserve ten free tickets, which staff fear will create empty blocks or informal resale. Requiring an account would reduce repeated reservations but conflicts with our no-account principle. The provider can cap each contact method at four tickets and send a simple confirmation request the day before. Families and small groups say four may be too low.

[Turn 9] ASSISTANT:
Use a household-sized cap and a separate assisted path for larger groups rather than introducing an account solely to police scarcity. Make cancellation easy, release unconfirmed capacity gradually, and watch whether the confirmation step disproportionately removes people with limited connectivity. Free access can still require fair-use rules, but the enforcement mechanism should not create a larger barrier than the behavior it prevents.

[Turn 10] USER:
The tourism office offered to place reservation links in hotel newsletters and at the airport. That could distribute demand across the day, but neighborhood organizations worry visitors will capture advance slots before residents hear about them. We do not have a resident category and do not want one. I am tempted to reject the tourism offer simply because it will make the reservation channel more successful than the assisted community block.

[Turn 10] ASSISTANT:
Do not suppress tourism promotion just to balance the channels. Stagger releases, preserve walk-in and same-day capacity, and publish the same information through libraries, community partners, and the entrance. Review distribution without creating a residency test.

[Turn 11] USER:
The fire marshal has now reduced safe occupancy after observing how people actually move through the exhibition. Staff say that proves timed entry is necessary. A trustee says it proves the forty-percent walk-in floor is too generous because unused reservations can always be released later. I think the second conclusion uses the safety change to protect the reservation system before it has produced evidence. Returned slots are uncertain; a walk-in floor is dependable. But I also understand that a fixed percentage means fewer total reservations now, and the outside queue could itself become a safety and weather problem. I do not want to defend forty percent because it is the number we already wrote down. I want to know whether the reason for it still holds under the new capacity.

[Turn 11] ASSISTANT:
Recalculate all channel counts using the new safety limit while preserving the agreed proportion unless evidence shows it is unworkable. Returned reservations are not equivalent to dependable walk-in capacity because their timing is uncertain. If crowding creates unsafe queues outside, use same-day timed walk-in tickets and the early adjustment rule rather than quietly reallocating access before observation.

[Turn 12] USER:
We will keep the forty-percent walk-in share under the revised occupancy, add same-day return times at the desk and by phone, use staggered reservation releases, and set a household-sized cap with assisted booking for larger groups. Promotion will go through tourism and neighborhood channels at the same time. We will count immediate entry, offered return times, abandoned visits, confirmations, and released capacity separately. The ten-week contract, privacy limits, weekly publication, and early walk-in adjustment remain unchanged.

[Turn 12] ASSISTANT:
The final design now responds to visitor behavior rather than forcing people into “planner” and “walk-in” categories. It protects immediate access, offers reliable same-day returns, staggers advance release, and handles larger groups without requiring accounts or residency tests. It also keeps the fire marshal's safety adjustment from silently rewriting the access promise before observation. Preserve the baseline finding that many walk-ins had planned their visit, the booking-page test, confirmation losses, promotion channels, revised occupancy, outside-queue conditions, and every allocation change. The board should see who waited, who returned, who abandoned the visit, and which channel actually worked for whom—not merely whether galleries looked calmer or the reservation system filled its slots.
